revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Bake Sale Cookies
revealWordProblem.text: Chef Academy is prepping for a bake sale. The classic cookie recipe makes 12 cookies using 3 cups of flour and 2 cups of sugar. The class wants to bake enough dough to make 60 cookies while keeping the recipe proportional. How many cups of flour and how many cups of sugar are needed? Explain your reasoning.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The scale factor is 60 ÷ 12 = 5. Multiply each ingredient by 5: flour = 3 × 5 = 15 cups, and sugar = 2 × 5 = 10 cups. The dough stays proportional because both ingredients were scaled by the same factor of 5.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do we use ratio reasoning to solve problems?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Find the scale factor, then multiply both parts; cross-multiply to check a proportion — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Chef Reyes's recipe serves 8 people and uses 5 cups of tomatoes. The banquet has 120 guests.
I find the scale factor: 120 divided by 8 = 15.
I multiply the tomatoes by 15: 5 x 15 = 75 cups of tomatoes.
To check, I can cross-multiply 5/8 = 75/120: 5 x 120 = 600 and 8 x 75 = 600.
The cross products match, so 75 cups is correct.

discourse.prompt: How can you TEST whether a pair of ratios is equivalent instead of guessing? Which pair was the trickiest to sort, and why?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I checked whether both parts of ___ were multiplied by the same number to get ___; the pair ___ is / is not equivalent because ___.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Chef Reyes wrote several pairs of ratios on the board. Sort them: which pairs are equivalent ratios (proportions) and which are NOT equivalent? As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

onLevel.stem: A chef uses the proportion 3/7 = x/28 to scale a recipe. What is x?
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Scale factor: 28 ÷ 7 = 4.
This uses a scale factor of 3, but the denominator did not triple. Divide 28 by 7 to see how many times larger the new denominator really is.
21 is 28 − 7, a subtracting move. Proportions grow by multiplying both parts by the same factor.
hints: Look at the bottoms of the fractions first: the 7 became 28.
Divide 28 by 7 to find the scale factor, then multiply the top number 3 by that same factor.
Compute 28 ÷ 7, then multiply 3 by the result to get x.
onLevel.stemEs: Un chef usa la proporción 3/7 = x/28 para ajustar una receta. ¿Cuánto vale x?
onLevel.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Multiplica: 3 × 4 = 12. Entonces x = 12.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Set up the proportion
workedExample.work: A recipe uses 4 cups of sugar for every 9 cups of flour: 4/9 = x/27.

onLevel.correctWork: Multiply by the scale factor instead of adding it: 4 × 3 = 12 cups of sugar. To keep ratios equivalent you multiply both parts by the scale factor — you never add it.
hints: Look at Step 3. The scale factor of 3 is correct, but what operation should you use with it?
To scale a ratio you MULTIPLY both parts by the factor (4 × 3), you do not add (4 + 3).
onLevel.explanation: The solving step added the scale factor instead of multiplying by it. Because 27 is 9 × 3, the sugar has to grow the same way: 4 × 3 = 12 cups. Adding would break the relationship, since 7/27 is not equivalent to 4/9 but 12/27 is.
onLevel.explanationEs: El paso de resolver sumó el factor de escala en vez de multiplicar por él. Como 27 es 9 × 3, el azúcar tiene que crecer igual: 4 × 3 = 12 tazas. Sumar rompería la relación, porque 7/27 no es equivalente a 4/9, pero 12/27 sí lo es.

onLevel.title: Find Priya's Mistake
onLevel.correctWork: 5 × 4 = 20 (multiply by the scale factor, don't add it)
hints: Look at Step 3. Priya found the correct scale factor of 4, but what did she do with it?
To keep ratios equivalent, multiply both parts by the scale factor — do NOT add.
onLevel.explanation: In the solving step Priya added the scale factor to 5 instead of multiplying by it. Since 32 is 8 × 4, the top of the fraction scales the same way: 5 × 4 = 20, so x = 20 and 20/32 simplifies right back to 5/8.
onLevel.explanationEs: En el paso de resolver, Priya sumó el factor de escala a 5 en vez de multiplicar por él. Como 32 es 8 × 4, la parte de arriba de la fracción se escala igual: 5 × 4 = 20, así que x = 20 y 20/32 se simplifica de nuevo a 5/8.

onLevel.stem: A recipe serves 6 people and uses 4 cups of rice. You need to serve 15 people. Show two different methods to find how much rice you need: (1) using a scale factor and (2) using a unit rate.
onLevel.sampleAnswer: Method 1 (scale factor): 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5. Multiply rice by 2.5: 4 × 2.5 = 10 cups. Method 2 (unit rate): 4 ÷ 6 = 2/3 cup per person. For 15 people: 2/3 × 15 = 10 cups. Both methods give 10 cups of rice.
onLevel.hint: Remember to explain which type each ratio is.
hints: You need the SAME answer two ways: once using a scale factor, once using a unit rate.
Method 1: scale factor = 15 ÷ 6, then multiply the rice. Method 2: rice per person = 4 ÷ 6, then multiply by 15 people.
Start Method 1: divide 15 ÷ 6 (it won't be whole — that's fine), then multiply 4 cups by it. Then try Method 2 and compare.
onLevel.stemEs: Una receta alcanza para 6 personas y usa 4 tazas de arroz. Necesitas servir a 15 personas. Muestra dos métodos distintos para hallar cuánto arroz necesitas: (1) usando un factor de escala y (2) usando una tasa por unidad.
onLevel.explanation: Both methods land on 10 cups. Scale factor: 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5, and 4 × 2.5 = 10. Unit rate: 4 ÷ 6 = 2/3 cup per person, and 2/3 × 15 = 10. The two methods agree because scaling a ratio and using its unit rate describe the very same relationship.
onLevel.explanationEs: Ambos métodos llegan a 10 tazas. Factor de escala: 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5, y 4 × 2.5 = 10. Tasa por unidad: 4 ÷ 6 = 2/3 de taza por persona, y 2/3 × 15 = 10. Los dos métodos coinciden porque escalar una razón y usar su tasa por unidad describen exactamente la misma relación.

extending.stem: Chef Reyes's pasta dough uses 2 eggs for every 3 cups of flour. For a banquet, the kitchen mixes 9 cups of flour. How many eggs are needed to keep the same ratio?
extending.explanation: Scale factor: 9 cups divided by 3 cups = 3. Multiply the eggs by the same factor: 2 x 3 = 6 eggs.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Scale factor: 9 cups divided by 3 cups = 3.
It looks like 6 was added to the 2 eggs. Ratios stay equal when both quantities are multiplied by the same factor, not when the same amount is added to each.
This doubles the eggs, but the flour did not double. Compare 9 cups to 3 cups to find the factor the recipe actually grew by.
extending.stemEs: La masa de pasta del chef Reyes usa 2 huevos por cada 3 tazas de harina. Para un banquete, la cocina mezcla 9 tazas de harina. ¿Cuántos huevos se necesitan para mantener la misma razón?
extending.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 9 tazas dividido entre 3 tazas = 3. Multiplica los huevos por el mismo factor: 2 x 3 = 6 huevos.
hints: Equivalent ratios keep the same relationship between eggs and flour, no matter how much dough you make.
Find the scale factor first: how many times larger is 9 cups than 3 cups?
The flour was multiplied by 3, so multiply the 2 eggs by 3 as well and see what you get.
hintsEs: Las razones equivalentes mantienen la misma relación entre huevos y harina, sin importar cuánta masa hagas.
Primero halla el factor de escala: ¿cuántas veces más grande es 9 tazas que 3 tazas?
La harina se multiplicó por 3, así que multiplica también los 2 huevos por 3 y observa qué obtienes.

extending.stem: A marinara recipe uses 4 cups of tomatoes for every 6 servings. The chef needs 18 servings. How many cups of tomatoes should she use?
extending.explanation: Scale factor: 18 servings divided by 6 servings = 3. Multiply the tomatoes by 3: 4 x 3 = 12 cups.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Scale factor: 18 servings divided by 6 servings = 3.
That is 4 + 12, an adding move. Equivalent ratios come from multiplying both quantities by the same factor.
This number does not come from the recipe's ratio. Work out how many times larger 18 servings is than 6 servings, then apply that factor to the 4 cups.
extending.stemEs: Una receta de salsa marinara usa 4 tazas de tomates por cada 6 porciones. La chef necesita 18 porciones. ¿Cuántas tazas de tomates debe usar?
extending.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 18 porciones dividido entre 6 porciones = 3. Multiplica los tomates por 3: 4 x 3 = 12 tazas.
hints: The ratio of tomatoes to servings has to stay the same as the batch grows.
Compare the new number of servings with the old one to find the scale factor.
18 servings is 3 times 6 servings, so multiply the 4 cups by that same factor.
hintsEs: La razón entre tomates y porciones debe seguir igual aunque la tanda crezca.
Compara el nuevo número de porciones con el original para hallar el factor de escala.
18 porciones es 3 veces 6 porciones, así que multiplica las 4 tazas por ese mismo factor.

extending.stem: During a cooking-team relay, a chef plates 3 finished dishes for every 5 minutes she works. At the same rate, how many dishes will she plate in 20 minutes?
extending.explanation: Scale factor: 20 minutes divided by 5 minutes = 4. Multiply the dishes by 4: 3 x 4 = 12 dishes.
choiceFeedback: Re-check how many times you need to multiply or scale.
That is 3 × 5, which multiplies the two parts of the ratio together. The scale factor comes from comparing 20 minutes with 5 minutes.
That is 3 + 5, an adding move. Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying both quantities by the same factor.
extending.stemEs: Durante un relevo de equipos de cocina, una chef emplata 3 platos terminados por cada 5 minutos que trabaja. Al mismo ritmo, ¿cuántos platos emplatará en 20 minutos?
extending.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 20 minutos dividido entre 5 minutos = 4. Multiplica los platos por 4: 3 x 4 = 12 platos.
hints: Working 'at the same rate' means the ratio of dishes to minutes does not change.
Find the scale factor by comparing 20 minutes with the 5 minutes in the given ratio.
20 minutes is 4 times 5 minutes, so multiply the 3 dishes by that same factor.
hintsEs: Trabajar 'al mismo ritmo' significa que la razón entre platos y minutos no cambia.
Halla el factor de escala comparando 20 minutos con los 5 minutos de la razón dada.
20 minutos es 4 veces 5 minutos, así que multiplica los 3 platos por ese mismo factor.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — Catch the Scaling Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the recipe
workedExample.work: Bread dough uses 7 cups of flour for every 2 eggs.

workedExample.label: Find the scale factor
workedExample.work: The chef needs 21 cups of flour. 21 divided by 7 = 3.

workedExample.label: Write the eggs
workedExample.work: Eggs stay at 2, so use 2 eggs.

extending.correctWork: Multiply the eggs by the SAME scale factor of 3: 2 x 3 = 6 eggs. Both parts of the ratio must be scaled, not just the flour.
hints: The flour was multiplied by 3, but what happened to the eggs?
To keep a ratio equivalent, scale BOTH parts by the same factor. If flour x 3, then eggs x 3 too.
extending.titleEs: Extensión de Nivel 2: atrapa el error de escala
extending.explanation: The last step kept the eggs at 2 even though the flour had just been multiplied by the scale factor of 3. A ratio stays equivalent only when both parts are scaled the same way, so the eggs become 2 × 3 = 6 and the recipe reads 21 cups of flour to 6 eggs.
extending.explanationEs: El último paso dejó los huevos en 2 aunque la harina acababa de multiplicarse por el factor de escala 3. Una razón se mantiene equivalente solo cuando las dos partes se escalan igual, así que los huevos llegan a 2 × 3 = 6 y la receta queda en 21 tazas de harina por 6 huevos.

extending.stem: A recipe uses 4 cups of broth for every 10 servings. How many cups of broth are needed for 30 servings?
extending.explanation: Scale factor: 30 ÷ 10 = 3. Multiply broth by 3: 4 × 3 = 12 cups.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Scale factor: 30 ÷ 10 = 3.
That is 4 + 10, an adding move. Equivalent ratios are built by multiplying both quantities by the same factor, not by adding the same amount to each.
You multiplied 4 by 10, the number of servings in the recipe, instead of by the scale factor. First find how many times larger 30 servings is than 10 servings.
hints: The servings jumped from 10 to 30 — the broth must grow by the same factor.
Find the scale factor by dividing the new servings by the recipe's servings, then multiply the broth by it.
Divide 30 ÷ 10 to get the scale factor — then multiply 4 cups of broth by that number.
extending.stemEs: Una receta usa 4 tazas de caldo por cada 10 porciones. ¿Cuántas tazas de caldo se necesitan para 30 porciones?
extending.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 30 ÷ 10 = 3. Multiplica el caldo por 3: 4 × 3 = 12 tazas.

extending.explanation: Divide 6:9 by 3 to get 2:3. Since both ratios simplify to 2:3, they are equivalent.
choiceFeedback: Scale both numbers by the same factor to make an equivalent ratio.
Not quite. Since both ratios simplify to ___:___, they are equivalent.
Subtracting the two parts is not the test for equivalent ratios. Two ratios are equivalent when one can be multiplied or divided by the same number to become the other.
hints: Two ratios are equivalent when one simplifies (or scales) exactly into the other.
Try dividing both parts of 6:9 by the same number — adding or subtracting the parts proves nothing about ratios.
Divide the 6 by 3 and the 9 by 3, then compare what you get with 2:3.
extending.explanationEs: Divide 6:9 entre 3 para obtener 2:3. Como ambas razones se simplifican a 2:3, son equivalentes.

extending.stem: If 3 pounds of apples cost $6, how much do 7 pounds cost?
extending.explanation: Unit rate: $6 ÷ 3 = $2 per pound. For 7 pounds: $2 × 7 = $14.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Unit rate: $6 ÷ 3 = $2 per pound.
It looks like $4 was added for the 4 extra pounds, but a pound costs more than $1. Find the price of a single pound first, then multiply.
That is 3 × 7, which multiplies the two given amounts together. Divide first to find the cost of one pound, then scale up.
hints: 7 pounds isn't a neat multiple of 3 pounds, so find the price of ONE pound first.
Unit rate: divide the $6 by the 3 pounds, then multiply the per-pound price by 7.
Divide 6 ÷ 3 to find dollars per pound — then multiply that price by 7 pounds.
extending.stemEs: Si 3 libras de manzanas cuestan $6, ¿cuánto cuestan 7 libras?
extending.explanationEs: Tasa por unidad: $6 ÷ 3 = $2 por libra. Para 7 libras: $2 × 7 = $14.

extending.stem: Solve the proportion: 2/5 = x/20. What is x?
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Scale factor: 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
4 is the scale factor that takes 5 to 20, not the value of x. You still have to apply that factor to the 2.
This comes from adding rather than multiplying. Find how many times larger 20 is than 5, then multiply the 2 by that same number.
hints: Look at the denominators first: the 5 grew into 20.
Find what number multiplies 5 into 20, then multiply the numerator 2 by that same number.
Divide 20 ÷ 5 to get the scale factor — then multiply 2 by it to find x.
extending.stemEs: Resuelve la proporción: 2/5 = x/20. ¿Cuánto vale x?
extending.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Multiplica: 2 × 4 = 8. Entonces x = 8.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Use Ratio Reasoning is scaling by adding instead of multiplying: since the banquet has 120 − 8 = 112 more guests than the recipe serves, some students add 112 to the ingredient amount instead of finding the scale factor. For Chef Reyes's recipe that serves 8 people with 5 cups of tomatoes, scaling up to 120 guests this way gives 5 + 112 = 117 cups of tomatoes — a wildly wrong answer. Ratios scale multiplicatively, not additively: find the scale factor first (120 ÷ 8 = 15), then multiply the ingredient by that same scale factor: 5 × 15 = 75 cups of tomatoes. Before you submit, check that you multiplied every part of the ratio by the same scale factor instead of adding the same amount to each.

connect.scenario: A school garden grows tomatoes. The gardeners know that 4 tomato plants produce about 20 tomatoes. The school wants to grow 100 tomatoes for a salsa-making event. They need to use ratio reasoning to determine how many plants to grow.
connect.prompt: This is like our ratio reasoning work because ___ and ___ are related by ___.

check.stem: How many tomatoes does one plant produce?
How many plants are needed for 100 tomatoes?
check.explanation: 100 ÷ 5 = 20 plants. You can also scale the ratio 4:20 up by 5 to get 20:100.

check.stem: What is the scale factor from 20 tomatoes to 100 tomatoes?
check.explanation: 100 ÷ 20 = 5. Multiply the plants by that same 5: 4 × 5 = 20 plants.

connect.modelAnswer: 4 plants produce 20 tomatoes, which is 5 tomatoes per plant. To reach 100 tomatoes, scale the ratio 4:20 up by 100 ÷ 20 = 5, giving 20:100 — so the school needs 20 plants.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — A recipe calls for 6 cups of flour for every 15 cookies. How many cups of flour are needed to make 45 cookies?
exitTicket.explanation: Scale factor: 45 ÷ 15 = 3. Multiply flour by 3: 6 × 3 = 18 cups of flour.
choiceFeedback: Find the scale factor: 15 × ? = 45, then apply it to the flour.
Recheck the multiplier — 45 ÷ 15 tells how many times to scale.
You added instead of scaling — multiply 6 by the right factor.
hints: 45 cookies is a scaled-up batch of the 15-cookie recipe — the flour must scale the same way.
Find the scale factor by dividing the new cookie count by the recipe's cookie count, then multiply the flour by it.
Divide 45 ÷ 15 to get the scale factor — then multiply 6 cups of flour by that number.

questions.stem: Which lemonade recipe is more lemony? Recipe A: 2 lemons for 6 cups of water. Recipe B: 3 lemons for 7 cups of water.
questions.explanation: Recipe A: 2÷6 ≈ 0.33 lemons per cup. Recipe B: 3÷7 ≈ 0.43 lemons per cup. Since 0.43 > 0.33, Recipe B is more lemony.

questions.stem: Chef A uses 2 cups of cheese for every 8 crackers. Chef B uses 3 cups of cheese for every 9 crackers. Who uses more cheese per cracker?
